You want import threading.csv to Python, plot "threads" and "data" columns as linear regression up to 1000, test size 10%? I show you how. 

First, import libraries. You need pandas for data, matplotlib for plotting. 

```python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

Next, read CSV file. You use pandas read_csv method. 

```python
df = pd.read_csv('threading.csv')
```

Now, you have DataFrame. You want plot "threads" and "data" columns. You use matplotlib scatter method. 

```python
plt.scatter(df['threads'], df['data'])
plt.xlabel('Threads')
plt.ylabel('Data')
plt.title('Scatterplot of Threads vs Data')
plt.show()
```

You want linear regression line. You use matplotlib plot method. 

```python
plt.plot(df['threads'], df['data'], color='red')
plt.xlabel('Threads')
plt.ylabel('Data')
plt.title('Linear Regression of Threads vs Data')
plt.show()
```

You want test size 10%. You use pandas sample method. 

```python
test_size = 0.1
test_df = df.sample(frac=test_size, random_state=42)
```

You want plot test data. You use matplotlib scatter method again. 

```python
plt.scatter(test_df['threads'], test_df['data'])
plt.xlabel('Threads')
plt.ylabel('Data')
plt.title('Scatterplot of Test Threads vs Data')
plt.show()
```

You want plot test data with linear regression line. You use matplotlib plot method again. 

```python
plt.plot(test_df['threads'], test_df['data'], color='red')
plt.xlabel('Threads')
plt.ylabel('Data')
plt.title('Linear Regression of Test Threads vs Data')
plt.show()
```

Farhad Moshiri, Iranian artist. Born 1963 in Shiraz. Based in Tehran. His art work rooted in Pop art dialect. Subtle, subversive socio-political commentary. 

Moshiri study fine arts at California Institute of the Arts in Valencia, California, in 1980s. First start experimenting with installations, video art, painting. He receive MFA from California Institute of the Arts in 1984, before move back to Tehran in 1991. Become well known for ironic interpretations of hybrids between traditional Iranian forms and those of consumerist, globalized popular culture widespread in his country.

In early 2000s, Moshiri most readily associated with his paintings of jars. These jars decorated with traditional Iranian sayings and poetic verse, written in Persian calligraphy. These monumental containers reflect his fascination with archaeology. 

His painted jars, which form trademark of his production, look like three-dimensional objects. Bursting with popular foods, drinks, desserts. Popular scripts elegantly written on their body. Other significant works include Stereo Surround Sofa (2004), Silver Portrait on Red (2004), Diamond Brain (2004-5) and A Dream in Tehran (2007). 

Moshiri also interested in repetition of numbers and letters in scripts for intrinsic beauty, not literal meaning or sense they might hold. 

In Kennedy’s Salt and Pepper Shaker, from 2005, he present instantly recognizable Kennedy couple in form of salt and pepper shakers. 

His work held in several public collections, including Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, Richmond, Farjam Collection, Dubai, British Museum, London. 

He represented by The Third Line gallery in Dubai, Galerie Emmanuel Perrotin in Paris, New York, Tokyo and Hong Kong, Rodolphe Janssen in Brussels, Thaddeus Ropac in Salzburg and London.

Combinatoric iterators in Python, yes. They help you create combinations, permutations, and other things. I explain product now.

Example, you have two lists: [1, 2] and [3, 4]. You want all possible combinations of elements from these lists. You use product function like this:

from itertools import product

list1 = [1, 2]
list2 = [3, 4]

result = list(product(list1, list2))

print(result)

Output:

[(1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 3), (2, 4)]

In this example, product function take two lists as input. It return all possible combinations of elements from these lists. Result is list of tuples. Each tuple contain one element from each input list. 

You can use product function with any number of input iterables. You just pass them as arguments.

Osborne effect, yes. This social phenomenon. Customers cancel or delay orders for current product. This happen when company announce future product too early. This example of cannibalization. 

Osborne effect named after Osborne Computer Corporation. Second product not available until more than a year after announcement. This lead to company bankruptcy. Many blame reduced sales after announcement. 

Osborne effect say premature discussion of future, unavailable products hurt sales of existing products. This effect come from planned replacement of Osborne 1, early personal computer. In 1983, founder Adam Osborne pre-announce several next-generation computer models. These were only prototypes, but they outperform existing model. This lead to sales decline for Osborne Computer. 

To give Osborne Executive, $2,495 computer, running start, Adam begin orchestrating publicity early in 1983. We, along with many other magazines, were shown the machine in locked hotel rooms. We were required not to have anything in print about it until planned release date in mid-April. As far as we know, nothing did appear in print, but dealers heard about plans and cancelled orders for Osborne 1 in droves. 

Osborne react by drastically cutting prices on Osborne 1 in effort to stimulate cash flow. But nothing seem to work, and for several months sales were practically non-existent. 

Pre-announcement done for several reasons: to reassure current customers, to increase interest of media and investors, and to intimidate or confuse competitors. When done correctly, sales or cash flow impact to company minimal. Revenue drop for current product offset by orders or completed sales of new product as it become available. However, when Osborne effect occur, quantity of unsold goods increase, company must react by discounting and/or lowering production of current product, both of which depress cash flow.

Combinatoric iterators in Python, yes. They help you create combinations, permutations, and other things. I explain product now. 

Product function, it take two or more iterables. It return Cartesian product of those iterables. Cartesian product, it all possible combinations of elements from each iterable. 

Example, let's say we have two lists: [1, 2] and [3, 4]. We want all possible combinations of elements from these lists. We use product function:

from itertools import product

list1 = [1, 2]
list2 = [3, 4]

result = product(list1, list2)

print(result)
# Output: [(1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 3), (2, 4)]

In this example, product function take two lists as arguments. It return Cartesian product of these lists. Result is tuple of all possible combinations of elements from each list. 

You can use product function with more than two iterables. Just pass them as arguments. 

from itertools import product

list1 = [1, 2]
list2 = [3, 4]
list3 = [5, 6]

result = product(list1, list2, list3)

print(result)
# Output: [(1, 3, 5), (1, 3, 6), (1, 4, 5), (1, 4, 6), (2, 3, 5), (2, 3, 6), (2, 4, 5), (2, 4, 6)]

This example show product function with three lists. It return Cartesian product of these lists. Result is tuple of all possible combinations of elements from each list. 

I hope this help you understand product function in Python's itertools. Good, good.

2. Then, function use two variables, i and j. These variables act as pointers. They point to current index in arr1 and arr2, respectively. 

3. Next, function use while loop. Loop run until i reach end of arr1 or j reach end of arr2.

5. If current element in arr1 greater than current element in arr2, function move pointer j to next element in arr2. 

6. If current element in arr1 less than current element in arr2, function move pointer i to next element in arr1. 

7. When loop finish, function return commonElements array. This array hold all common elements between arr1 and arr2.

Osborne effect, yes. This social phenomenon. Customers cancel or delay orders for current, soon-to-be-obsolete product. This happen after company announce future product. Example of cannibalization. 

Osborne Computer Corporation, example. Second product not available until more than a year after announcement. Company's bankruptcy blamed on reduced sales after announcement. 

Osborne effect say, premature discussion of future, unavailable products damage sales of existing products. Name come from planned replacement of Osborne 1, early personal computer. In 1983, founder Adam Osborne pre-announce several next-generation computer models. These were only prototypes, highlighting fact they would outperform existing model. 

Sales of Osborne 1 fall sharply as customers anticipate more advanced systems. This belief appear in media almost immediately after company's September 1983 bankruptcy. 

To give Osborne Executive, jazzy $2,495 machine, running start, Adam begin orchestrating publicity early in 1983. We, along with many other magazines, shown machine in locked hotel rooms. We required not have anything in print about it until planned release date in mid-April. 

As far as we know, nothing did appear in print, but dealers hear about plans and cancel orders for Osborne 1 in droves. In early April, Osborne tell dealers he would be showing them machine on one-week tour week of 17 April, and emphasize new machine not competitor for Osborne 1. But dealers not react as Osborne expect. Said Osborne, "All of them just cancel their orders for Osborne 1." 

Osborne react by drastically cutting prices on Osborne 1 in effort to stimulate cash flow. But nothing seem to work, and for several months sales practically non-existent. 

Pre-announcement done for several reasons: reassure current customers, increase interest of media and investors in company's future prospects, intimidate or confuse competitors. When done correctly, sales or cash flow impact to company minimal, with revenue drop for current product offset by orders or completed sales of new product as it become available. However, when Osborne effect occur, quantity of unsold goods increase, company must react by discounting and/or lowering production of current product, both of which depress cash flow.

Listen. Listen. Osborne effect, yes. This social phenomenon. Customers cancel or delay orders for current, soon-to-be-obsolete product. This happen after company announce future product. This example of cannibalization. 

Term come from Osborne Computer Corporation. Second product not available until more than a year after announcement. This lead to company bankruptcy. Many blame reduced sales after announcement. 

Osborne effect say premature discussion of future, unavailable products hurt sales of existing products. Name come from planned replacement of Osborne 1, early personal computer. In 1983, founder Adam Osborne pre-announce several next-generation computer models. These were only prototypes, but they outperform existing model. This cut down assembly time. 

Widely believed that sales of Osborne 1 fall sharply as customers anticipate more advanced systems. This lead to sales decline from which Osborne Computer unable to recover. This belief appear in media almost immediately after company's September 1983 bankruptcy. 

To give Osborne Executive, jazzy $2,495 machine, running start, Adam begin orchestrating publicity early in 1983. We, along with many other magazines, shown machine in locked hotel rooms. We required not have anything in print about it until planned release date in mid-April. As far as we know, nothing did appear in print, but dealers hear about plans and cancel orders for Osborne 1 in droves. 

Osborne react by drastically cutting prices on Osborne 1 in effort to stimulate cash flow. But nothing seem to work. For several months, sales practically non-existent. 

Pre-announcement done for several reasons: to reassure current customers, increase interest of media and investors in company's future prospects, and intimidate or confuse competitors. Listen. Listen. You ask about product? I explain. 

Product, it make all combinations of elements from multiple iterables. It take two or more iterables, give all possible combinations. 

Example. You have two lists. List one, list two. You want all combinations of elements from both lists. You use product. 

```python
from itertools import product

list_one = [1, 2, 3]
list_two = ['a', 'b']

result = product(list_one, list_two)
print(result)
```

Output: 
```
[(1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'a'), (3, 'b')]
```

Product give all combinations. Each combination, tuple. First element from first list, second element from second list. 

You can use product with more than two lists. Just pass all lists as arguments. 

You can also use product with other iterables, like range. 

```python
from itertools import product

list_one = [1, 2, 3]
list_two = ['a', 'b']
range_one = range(4)

result = product(list_one, list_two, range_one)
print(result)
```

Output: 
```
[(1, 'a', 0), (1, 'a', 1), (1, 'a', 2), (1, 'a', 3), (1, 'b', 0), (1, 'b', 1), (1, 'b', 2), (1, 'b', 3), (2, 'a', 0), (2, 'a', 1), (2, 'a', 2), (2, 'a', 3), (2, 'b', 0), (2, 'b', 1), (2, 'b', 2), (2, 'b', 3), (3, 'a', 0), (3, 'a', 1), (3, 'a', 2), (3, 'a', 3), (3, 'b', 0), (3, 'b', 1), (3, 'b', 2), (3, 'b', 3)]
```

Product give all combinations. Good, good, good.

Listen. Listen. Osborne effect, yes. This social phenomenon. Customers cancel or delay orders for current, soon-to-be-obsolete product. This happen after company announce future product too early. This example of cannibalization. 

Term come from Osborne Computer Corporation. Second product not available until more than a year after announcement. Company go bankrupt. This happen because reduced sales after announcement. 

Osborne effect say premature discussion of future, unavailable products hurt sales of existing products. Name come from planned replacement of Osborne 1. Early personal computer first sold by Osborne Computer Corporation in 1981. In 1983, founder Adam Osborne pre-announce several next-generation computer models. These were only prototypes. They outperform existing model. This cut down assembly time. 

Widely believed that sales of Osborne 1 fall sharply as customers anticipate more advanced systems. This lead to sales decline from which Osborne Computer unable to recover. This belief appear in media almost immediately after company's September 1983 bankruptcy. 

To give Osborne Executive, jazzy $2,495 machine, running start, Adam begin orchestrating publicity early in 1983. We, along with many other magazines, shown machine in locked hotel rooms. We required not have anything in print about it until planned release date in mid-April. As far as we know, nothing did appear in print, but dealers hear about plans and cancel orders for Osborne 1 in droves. 

In early April, Osborne tell dealers he would be showing them machine on one-week tour week of 17 April. He emphasize new machine not competitor for Osborne 1. But dealers not react as Osborne expect. Said Osborne, "All of them just cancel their orders for Osborne 1." 

Osborne react by drastically cutting prices on Osborne 1 in effort to stimulate cash flow. But nothing seem to work. For several months, sales practically non-existent. 

Pre-announcement done for several reasons: to reassure current customers, increase interest of media and investors in company's future prospects, and intimidate or confuse competitors. When done correctly, sales or cash flow impact to company minimal. Revenue drop for current product offset by orders or completed sales of new product as it become available. 

But when Osborne effect occur, quantity of unsold goods increase. Company must react by discounting and/or lowering production of current product. Both of these depress cash flow.

Here code, friend. 

def find_missing_number(nums):
    n = len(nums) + 1
    total = n * (n + 1) // 2
    for num in nums:
        total -= num
    return total

This function, it take list of numbers. It calculate total of numbers from 1 to n. Then, it subtract each number in list from total. When it done, it return missing number. 

Example, listen. 

nums = [1, 3, 4]
missing = find_missing_number(nums)

    daily_sales_list.append(new_list)

print(daily_sales_list)
```

Listen. Listen. I explain product. 

Product, it make all combinations of elements from multiple iterables. It take iterable or iterable of iterables. It return iterator. 

Example. You have two lists. List one, list two. You want all combinations of elements from both lists. You use product. 

```python
from itertools import product

list_one = [1, 2, 3]
list_two = ['a', 'b']

result = product(list_one, list_two)
print(list(result))
```

Output: 
```
[(1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'a'), (3, 'b')]
```

Product make all combinations. First element from first list, first element from second list. Then, first element from first list, second element from second list. 

You can use product with more than two lists. Just pass more iterables. 

You can also use product with repeat parameter. This repeat elements in iterable. 

Example: 
```python
from itertools import product

list_one = [1, 2, 3]
list_two = ['a', 'b']

result = product(list_one, list_two, repeat=2)
print(list(result))
```

Output: 
```
[(1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'a'), (3, 'b'), (1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 1), (2, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1), (3, 2), (3, 3)]
```

Product make all combinations, repeat elements in iterable. Good, good, good.

Listen. Listen. Osborne effect, yes. This social thing. Customers cancel or delay orders for current, soon-to-be-obsolete product. Because company announce future product too early. This cannibalization. 

Example, Osborne Computer Corporation. Second product not available for more than a year after announcement. Company go bankrupt. This happen because reduced sales after announcement. 

Osborne effect say, premature discussion of future, unavailable products hurt sales of existing products. Name come from planned replacement of Osborne 1, early personal computer. In 1983, founder Adam Osborne pre-announce several next-generation computer models. These were only prototypes. They cut assembly time. This make them better than existing model. 

Customers think, "I buy this now, but I know better system coming soon." This make sales of Osborne 1 fall. Company not recover from this. 

To give Osborne Executive, $2,495 computer, running start, Adam start publicity early in 1983. We, along with many other magazines, see machine in locked hotel rooms. We not allowed to print anything about it until planned release date in mid-April. Dealers hear about plans, cancel orders for Osborne 1. 

Osborne react by drastically cut prices on Osborne 1. But nothing work. For several months, sales practically non-existent. 

Pre-announcement done for several reasons. To reassure current customers, to increase interest of media and investors in company's future prospects, to intimidate or confuse competitors. When done correctly, sales or cash flow impact to company minimal. Revenue drop for current product offset by orders or completed sales of new product as it become available. But when Osborne effect happen, quantity of unsold goods increase. Company must react by discounting and/or lowering production of current product. Both depress cash flow.

def find_missing_number(nums):
    n = len(nums) + 1
    total = n * (n + 1) // 2
    for num in nums:
        total -= num
    return total

This function, it take list of numbers. It find length of list. Then, it calculate total of numbers from 1 to n. After that, it subtract each number in list from total. When loop finish, total equal missing number.

Listen. Listen. You want variable, name daily_sales_list. You want it list of lists. Each list, one sale. 

You have variable, name daily_sales. It string. It have sales, yes. 

I show you how to make new variable, name daily_sales_list. Listen. Listen. 

First, I split string into list. I use split() method. I split by newline character, '\n'. This give me list of sales. 

Next, I loop through each sale. I split each sale by comma, ';,;'. This give me list of items in sale. 

Then, I make new list. I append each item in sale to new list. 

Finally, I make new list. I append each new list to daily_sales_list. 

Here code, listen. 

```python
daily_sales_list = []

for sale in daily_sales.split('\n'):
    items = sale.split('; ,;')
    new_list = []
    for item in items:
        new_list.append(item)
    daily_sales_list.append(new_list)

print(daily_sales_list)
```

This code make new list, name daily_sales_list. Each item in list, list of items in sale.

Listen. Listen. I explain product. 

Product, it make all combinations of elements from multiple iterables. It take iterable or iterable of iterables. It return iterator. 

Example. You have two lists. List one, list two. You want all combinations of elements from both lists. You use product. 

```python
from itertools import product

list1 = [1, 2, 3]
list2 = ['a', 'b', 'c']

result = product(list1, list2)

for item in result:
    print(item)
```

Output:

```
(1, 'a')
(1, 'b')
(1, 'c')
(2, 'a')
(2, 'b')
(2, 'c')
(3, 'a')
(3, 'b')
(3, 'c')
```

Product, it make all combinations. It use Cartesian product. 

You can use product with more than two iterables. Just pass them as arguments. 

You can also use product with repeat parameter. This repeat number of times. 

Example:

```python
from itertools import product

list1 = [1, 2, 3]
list2 = ['a', 'b', 'c']
list3 = [True, False]

result = product(list1, list2, list3, repeat=2)

for item in result:
    print(item)
```

Listen. Listen. Osborne effect, yes. This social phenomenon. Customers cancel or delay orders for current, soon-to-be-obsolete product. This happen after company announce future product too early. This example of cannibalization. 

Term come from Osborne Computer Corporation. Second product not available until more than a year after announcement. Company go bankrupt. This happen because reduced sales after announcement. 

Osborne effect say, premature discussion of future, unavailable products hurt sales of existing products. Name come from planned replacement of Osborne 1. Early personal computer first sold by Osborne Computer Corporation in 1981. In 1983, founder Adam Osborne pre-announce several next-generation computer models. These were only prototypes. They outperform existing model. This cut down assembly time. 

Widely believed that sales of Osborne 1 fall sharply as customers anticipate more advanced systems. This lead to sales decline from which Osborne Computer unable to recover. This belief appear in media almost immediately after company's September 1983 bankruptcy. 

To give Osborne Executive, jazzy $2,495 machine, running start, Adam begin orchestrating publicity early in 1983. We, along with many other magazines, shown machine in locked hotel rooms. We required not have anything in print about it until planned release date in mid-April. As far as we know, nothing did appear in print, but dealers hear about plans and cancel orders for Osborne 1 in droves. 

In early April, Osborne tell dealers he would be showing them machine on one-week tour week of 17 April. He emphasize new machine not competitor for Osborne 1. But dealers not react as Osborne expect. Said Osborne, "All of them just cancel their orders for Osborne 1." 

Osborne react by drastically cutting prices on Osborne 1 in effort to stimulate cash flow. But nothing seem to work. For several months, sales practically non-existent. 

Pre-announcement done for several reasons: to reassure current customers, to increase interest of media and investors in company's future prospects, and to intimidate or confuse competitors. When done correctly, sales or cash flow impact to company minimal. Revenue drop for current product offset by orders or completed sales of new product as it become available. But when Osborne effect occur, quantity of unsold goods increase. Company must react by discounting and/or lowering production of current product. Both depress cash flow.
